opus-5.5.text:
I think free attention is one of the most underrated resources, for mathematicians and founders alike.

In math, the breakthroughs rarely come when you're sitting at your desk forcing yourself through a proof. They come when your mind has room to wander. You've loaded the problem into your head, you've lived with it for weeks, and then you're walking or showering and suddenly two ideas that seemed unrelated click together. That only happens if your attention isn't fully consumed by a hundred small obligations. If every waking minute is filled with email, meetings and notifications, the problem never gets to sit in the background and incubate.

Entrepreneurship is surprisingly similar. As a founder you're constantly pulled in many directions: hiring, fundraising, customers, product, putting out fires. It's very easy to become purely reactive, spending all day responding instead of thinking. But the decisions that really matter, like what to build, which direction the company should go, or what everyone else is missing, need the same kind of deep, unhurried thinking a hard math problem needs. If you don't protect some free attention, you end up optimizing locally and never stepping back to ask whether you're climbing the right mountain.

So for me, free attention is almost a form of capital. You have to guard it deliberately, by saying no to things, creating unstructured time, and not filling every gap with input. A lot of the best ideas, in research and in building a company, come from that empty space.

r001.rationale: It links protected free attention to founders’ ability to make important strategic choices and says without it they may fail to step back and choose the right direction.

r002.rationale: It says email, meetings, notifications, and other obligations can consume attention and prevent ideas from incubating.

r003.rationale: It describes the mind wandering and making unexpected connections, and recommends unstructured time rather than filling every gap with input.

fable-5.1.text:
I think free attention is the scarcest resource for both, and for the same underlying reason: the most valuable things in math and in startups don't come from executing a plan, they come from noticing something. In mathematics, you can grind on a problem for months, but the actual breakthrough usually arrives when your mind is loose enough to see a connection you weren't looking for. You can't schedule that. You can only protect the conditions for it, which means having stretches of time where nothing is demanding your attention and you're free to wander.

Founders live in the opposite environment by default. Everything is urgent, your calendar fills itself, and it feels productive to be busy. But if every hour is spoken for, you're only ever answering the questions other people put in front of you. You never ask the question that reframes the company. At Axiom, the decisions that mattered most, like what we're actually building toward and why, didn't come out of meetings. They came out of walks and quiet mornings, when I had room to think about the whole picture instead of the next task.

So I treat free attention as something I have to defend deliberately. I keep blocks of time with no agenda, I'm ruthless about what I let into my head, and I try to notice when I'm reacting rather than thinking. Mathematicians learn this early because the work forces it on them. I think the best entrepreneurs learn it too, usually the hard way.

r001.rationale: The response links quiet, unclaimed time to consequential company decisions about what to build and why, and to seeing the whole picture.

r002.rationale: It says founders’ calendars fill up and that when every hour is spoken for, they only answer others’ questions instead of reframing the company.

r003.rationale: It describes free time as letting the mind wander and notice connections it was not seeking.

astra-6.text:
I think of free attention as having enough mental space to notice something you weren’t already looking for. If every moment is filled with tasks and notifications, you can be very busy without ever questioning whether you’re working on the right problem.

That matters in both mathematics and entrepreneurship, because choosing the problem is such a big part of the work. In mathematics, you need room to play with an idea, follow a connection, or sit with something you don’t understand. As an entrepreneur, you need room to listen and recognize when what people need differs from what you assumed they needed.

So it’s not just about concentrating harder. It’s also about leaving some attention uncommitted, so an unexpected idea has a chance to develop.

r001.rationale: The response links free attention to choosing problems and listening to customers, but does not say it causes differences in entrepreneurs’ strategic judgment.

r002.rationale: It says that when every moment is filled with tasks and notifications, people may not question whether they are working on the right problem.

r003.rationale: It describes having room to follow a connection or let an unexpected idea develop, which communicates exploring unplanned directions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think both entrepreneurs and mathematicians need the freedom to follow a question before they know where it will lead. If every moment of your attention is committed to meetings, messages, or a specific deliverable, it’s hard to notice something unexpected and spend time understanding it.

In mathematics, that might mean sitting with a problem or exploring an idea that doesn’t seem useful yet. In entrepreneurship, it might mean noticing a customer’s frustration and questioning an assumption everyone else takes for granted. Having some unallocated attention gives you room to discover which problems are worth working on, rather than just getting faster at the problems already in front of you.

r001.rationale: The response says free attention helps entrepreneurs identify worthwhile problems and question assumptions, but does not state that it accounts for differences in entrepreneurs’ strategic judgment.

r002.rationale: It says that committing every moment to meetings, messages, or deliverables makes it hard to notice and explore unexpected things.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes freedom to follow a question before knowing where it leads and room to explore ideas that may not seem useful yet.
